chapters.1: Jesus gives final instructions to his apostles before ascending into heaven, promising they will receive the Holy Spirit and become his witnesses to the whole world. The disciples return to Jerusalem to wait and pray together, and they choose Matthias to replace Judas among the twelve apostles.
chapters.2: On the Day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit comes upon the disciples with wind and fire, enabling them to speak in other languages so that visitors from many nations understand them. Peter preaches boldly about Jesus' death and resurrection, about three thousand people believe and are baptized, and the new believers form a close-knit community that shares possessions and devotes itself to prayer and teaching.
chapters.3: Peter and John heal a man who had been lame from birth at the temple gate, and a crowd gathers in amazement. Peter uses the moment to preach about Jesus as the promised Messiah, urging the people to repent so their sins may be forgiven.
chapters.4: Peter and John are arrested and questioned by the religious council for healing in Jesus' name, but they boldly declare there is salvation in no other name and are released after the leaders fail to intimidate them. The believers pray for continued boldness, and the growing community continues sharing resources so that no one among them is in need.
chapters.5: A couple named Ananias and Sapphira die after lying to the apostles about money they secretly withheld from the church's common fund, bringing great fear on the believers. The apostles continue performing many healings, and after being arrested and miraculously freed from prison, they are brought before the council again, where the respected teacher Gamaliel persuades the leaders not to kill them.
chapters.6: The apostles appoint seven men, including Stephen, to manage practical care for the community so they can focus on preaching and prayer. Stephen becomes known for his wisdom and miracles, but is falsely accused of blasphemy and dragged before the religious council.
chapters.7: Stephen defends himself before the council with a long summary of Israel's history, showing how the people repeatedly resisted God's messengers, climaxing in their rejection of Jesus. His accusers become enraged and stone him to death, while he prays for their forgiveness as he dies, with a young man named Saul watching.
chapters.8: A wave of persecution scatters believers out from Jerusalem, and Philip preaches successfully in Samaria, where a sorcerer named Simon tries unsuccessfully to buy spiritual power. Philip is then led by the Spirit to explain the gospel to an Ethiopian official, who believes and is baptized.
chapters.9: Saul, a zealous persecutor of Christians, is dramatically confronted by the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus and is blinded, then healed and transformed by a disciple named Ananias. He begins preaching Christ despite suspicion from other believers, while Peter raises a woman named Tabitha from the dead in Joppa.
chapters.10: God gives Peter a vision showing that Gentiles should not be considered unclean, preparing him to visit the Roman centurion Cornelius, who has also received a vision. As Peter preaches to Cornelius's household, the Holy Spirit falls on them just as on the Jewish believers, showing that the gospel is for Gentiles too.
chapters.11: Peter explains to skeptical Jewish believers in Jerusalem how God clearly included the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit, and they accept that God has granted repentance to non-Jews as well. The gospel spreads to Antioch, where believers are first called Christians, and the church there sends relief to famine-stricken believers in Judea.
chapters.12: King Herod has the apostle James killed and imprisons Peter, but an angel miraculously frees Peter from prison the night before his scheduled execution. Herod later dies suddenly after accepting worship as though he were a god, while the word of God continues to spread.
chapters.13: The church at Antioch commissions Barnabas and Saul (now called Paul) for missionary work, and they travel through Cyprus and into Asia Minor preaching the gospel. In Antioch of Pisidia, Paul preaches a detailed sermon about Jesus fulfilling God's promises, and when many Jews reject the message, he and Barnabas turn to preach to the Gentiles instead.
chapters.14: Paul and Barnabas continue preaching through Lystra and Derbe, healing a crippled man and narrowly stopping the crowd from worshipping them as gods. Paul is later stoned and left for dead in Lystra but recovers, and the missionaries strengthen the new churches before returning to report to the church in Antioch.
chapters.15: A dispute arises over whether Gentile believers must follow Jewish law, and the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to resolve it. They conclude that Gentiles don't need to be circumcised, only asked to avoid a few specific practices, and Paul and Barnabas later part ways over a disagreement about taking John Mark on a new journey.
chapters.16: Paul, now traveling with Silas and young Timothy, is guided by a vision to preach in Macedonia, where Lydia becomes an early convert in Philippi. After Paul casts a spirit out of a slave girl, he and Silas are beaten and imprisoned, but an earthquake frees them and their faith leads the jailer and his household to believe.
chapters.17: Paul preaches in Thessalonica and Berea, facing opposition from some Jewish leaders but finding eager listeners among others. In Athens, he addresses the philosophers at the Areopagus, using their altar to an 'unknown god' as a way to introduce the true God and the resurrection of Jesus.
chapters.18: Paul settles in Corinth, working as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla while preaching, and stays over a year building up the church there despite opposition. He later travels on, encountering the eloquent teacher Apollos, who is further instructed in the faith by Aquila and Priscilla.
chapters.19: Paul spends significant time teaching in Ephesus, where disciples receive the Holy Spirit and remarkable miracles occur, leading many to abandon practices tied to sorcery. A riot breaks out among silversmiths who feel threatened by Paul's preaching against idol worship, but city officials calm the crowd.
chapters.20: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, at one point restoring to life a young man named Eutychus who fell asleep and dropped from a window during a long sermon. He then gives an emotional farewell address to the elders of Ephesus, warning them to guard the church and reminding them it is more blessed to give than to receive.
chapters.21: Despite warnings that he will face suffering in Jerusalem, Paul insists on going, and he is later seized by an angry mob in the temple after being falsely accused of defiling it. Roman soldiers rescue him from the crowd, and Paul asks permission to address the people.
chapters.22: Paul recounts his life story and dramatic conversion on the road to Damascus to the hostile Jerusalem crowd, but the mention of preaching to Gentiles reignites their fury. He is nearly flogged until he reveals he is a Roman citizen, which halts the proceedings.
chapters.23: Paul causes a dispute between Pharisees and Sadducees on the council by mentioning the resurrection, and he is removed for his safety when the argument turns violent. Learning of a plot to kill Paul, Roman officials transfer him under heavy guard to the governor Felix in Caesarea.
chapters.24: Paul is formally accused before Governor Felix of being a troublemaker, but he defends himself, explaining his beliefs about the resurrection and his innocence of any real crime. Felix, intrigued but also hoping for a bribe, leaves Paul in custody for two years without resolving the case.
chapters.25: The new governor, Festus, considers sending Paul back to Jerusalem to be tried, but Paul appeals to have his case heard by Caesar in Rome instead. King Agrippa visits and asks to hear Paul's case for himself, setting up his defense in the next chapter.
chapters.26: Paul gives a compelling account of his conversion and calling before King Agrippa, explaining that his message about Jesus' resurrection is rooted in the Hebrew Scriptures. Agrippa and the other officials conclude that Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment, though his earlier appeal to Caesar means he must still go to Rome.
chapters.27: Paul is placed on a ship bound for Rome, and despite his warning, the voyage runs into a violent storm that threatens to destroy the vessel. After many days adrift, Paul assures the crew that God will spare everyone's life, and the ship eventually wrecks near an island, with all 276 people aboard reaching land safely.
chapters.28: Paul and the survivors land on the island of Malta, where he is bitten by a venomous snake without harm and heals the sick, amazing the islanders. He eventually reaches Rome, where he spends two years under house arrest, freely preaching about Jesus to all who come to him.
